parts.next_up: Part 4 tackles something that still looks like magic: how a machine heavier than a truck full of bricks manages to fly, and stay up there, explained without any of the jargon.

parts.recap_so_far: So far you've decoded the engine that turns burning fuel into motion, the fridge trick of moving heat instead of making cold, and the split-second dance inside your phone. Today you're tackling the one that still looks like magic from the ground: how something built from metal, heavier than a blue whale, climbs into the sky and stays there.

chunks.heading: The flying whale problem
chunks.idea: A fully loaded jumbo jet can weigh more than a blue whale. Something built from sheet metal and jet fuel, with no wings that flap, somehow leaves the ground anyway — and it isn't because the engines are strong enough to punch it upward.
chunks.detail:
Picture something as heavy as a blue whale. Now picture it rolling down a strip of concrete, lifting its nose, and climbing calmly up to 35,000 feet. That is roughly what happens every time a big loaded jet takes off.

It feels like it should be impossible. Metal is heavy. Air is something you can't even see or feel unless it's moving fast. How does "basically nothing" hold up something so heavy?

Here's the twist: the engines are barely involved in the lifting. On a cruising jet, the engines are mostly pushing the plane forward, not up.

The actual lifting is being done by something much quieter — the wings. Shaped and tilted just right, they are constantly grabbing the air rushing past and doing one clever thing to it, over and over, thousands of times a second.

That one clever thing is the entire secret of flight. Once you see it, you will never look at a wing — or a bird, or a frisbee — quite the same way again.
chunks.example: A fully loaded Boeing 747 can weigh in the neighborhood of 400 tons at takeoff — several times heavier than the largest blue whale ever recorded. Every one of those tons gets carried into the sky by two thin wings meeting moving air, not by engines aimed downward like a rocket.
points: A jet's engines mostly push it forward, not up — the wings do the actual lifting.
The heaviest planes weigh hundreds of tons, yet climb using shaped surfaces meeting moving air, not brute force.
Flight isn't about outmuscling gravity — it's about air, used cleverly.
chunks.key_takeaway: A plane doesn't fly by overpowering gravity with power — its wings quietly put moving air to work.

key_terms.definition: The upward force a wing generates that balances a plane's weight and holds it in the air.

chunks.heading: Why a wing pushes air down — and gets pushed up
chunks.idea: You may have heard that air splits at the front of a wing and has to "race" to meet back up at the tail, and that this creates lift. NASA's own engineers say that popular story is wrong. The real trick is simpler: a wing shoves air downward, and the air shoves back.
chunks.detail:
Long before airplanes existed, Isaac Newton worked out a rule that happens to explain wings perfectly: every push has an equal push back. Shove something one way, and it shoves you back the other way.

A wing flies tilted very slightly upward into the oncoming air — engineers call this tilt the angle of attack. Because of that tilt, plus the wing's gentle curve, the wing shoves the air flowing over and under it downward and backward as the plane moves forward.

Since the wing just shoved a large mass of air downward, Newton's rule says the air must shove back on the wing — upward. That upward shove-back is lift.

Here's the popular myth you may already know: that air splits at the wing's leading edge, and the two streams must arrive at the trailing edge at the same instant, so the air flowing over the curved top has to speed up — and that speed somehow creates lift through lower pressure. NASA's aerodynamics engineers are blunt about this one: the streams don't actually reunite that way at all, and the explanation is simply not accurate.

The honest, simple version is the one above. Tilt a surface into oncoming air, throw that air downward, and the air throws you back upward. A wing is really just a very refined device for throwing air down.
chunks.example: Stick your flat hand out of a moving car window, if it's safe and legal where you are, and tilt your fingertips up just slightly. You'll feel your whole hand shove upward in the wind — that's the exact same push-back Newton described, just happening at hand-scale instead of wing-scale.
points: Newton's third law: push air one way, and the air pushes back the opposite way — that push-back is lift.
A wing's slight upward tilt (angle of attack) plus its curve is what shoves the passing air downward.
The popular "air races to meet up at the tail" story is a myth — NASA's own guide says it's not accurate.
More tilt, up to a point, means more air thrown down, and more lift pushed back.
chunks.key_takeaway: A wing makes lift by throwing air downward — and by Newton's third law, the air throws the wing back up.

key_terms.definition: The angle at which a wing is tilted into the oncoming airflow — the main dial a pilot uses to control how much lift a wing makes.
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction — the physics rule underneath how a wing generates lift.

chunks.heading: Tilt it too far and the air lets go
chunks.idea: Angle of attack is the main lift dial — tilt a wing up a little more and it makes more lift. But push that tilt too far, and the air can no longer follow the wing's shape at all. Lift can vanish, suddenly.
chunks.detail:
Tilt a wing up a little more, and it throws more air down, making more lift — which is part of why a plane's nose lifts slightly as it takes off.

But there's a limit. Air flowing over the curved top of a wing likes to hug that surface closely, flowing smoothly along it — engineers just call this attached flow.

Tilt the wing too steeply, and the air can no longer bend sharply enough to follow it. Instead of hugging the top, it breaks away into a churning, tumbling mess.

The instant that happens, lift collapses, sometimes suddenly. Pilots call this a stall, and it has nothing to do with the engine — the engine can be running perfectly while the wings themselves stall.

This is exactly why pilots watch their speed and nose angle so carefully near the ground, during takeoff and landing, when there is little height left to recover.
chunks.example: Hold your hand flat out the car window again and tilt it up more and more steeply. At a small tilt your hand rides smoothly upward on the wind; tilt it almost straight up and it starts buffeting and shaking instead of lifting cleanly — the air has stopped flowing smoothly over it. That shudder is a tiny, harmless version of a stall.
points: More tilt (angle of attack) means more lift — but only up to a critical limit.
Past that limit, air stops hugging the wing's top surface and tumbles instead — this sudden loss of lift is called a stall.
A stall is about airflow and angle, not engine power — the engine can be fine while the wing stalls.
Stalls are most dangerous close to the ground, which is why takeoff and landing get the most careful attention.
chunks.key_takeaway: Lift grows with tilt only up to a point — push past it, and the air stops following the wing, taking lift with it.

key_terms.definition: A sudden loss of lift that happens when a wing's angle of attack gets too steep and airflow over the top breaks away instead of staying smooth.

chunks.heading: The four-way tug of war
chunks.idea: Every flying plane is stuck in a constant four-way tug of war: lift pulls it up, weight pulls it down, thrust shoves it forward, and drag drags it back. Flight is really just this tug of war, held in careful balance.
chunks.detail:
Four forces act on a plane the entire time it flies. Lift pulls up, weight (gravity) pulls down, thrust — from the engines — pushes forward, and drag, which is just air resistance, pulls backward.

When lift exactly matches weight, and thrust exactly matches drag, the plane holds a steady altitude and speed. Nothing changes, even though four powerful forces are fighting the whole time underneath that calm.

Tip lift stronger than weight, even briefly, and the plane climbs. Let drag start beating thrust, and the plane slows down — and because a slower wing makes less lift, weight can then start winning too, so the plane sinks.

This is also why "no motion, no lift" matters so much. A wing only shoves air down, and only gets shoved back up, while air keeps flowing past it fast enough — slow down too much, and lift disappears no matter how the wing is tilted.

That's the real reason a normal airplane can't just hover in place like a helicopter can. A fixed wing must keep moving through the air to keep this whole tug of war going; a helicopter solves the problem differently, by spinning its rotor blades — which are really just thin, fast-spinning wings — even while the rest of the aircraft stays still.
chunks.example: A glider has no engine at all, so it has zero thrust fighting its drag — it is always slowly losing this tug of war and sinking through the air. A skilled glider pilot instead hunts for thermals, rising columns of warm air, and rides them upward faster than the glider naturally sinks, buying altitude for free.
points: Four forces always act on a flying plane: lift (up), weight (down), thrust (forward), drag (backward).
Steady, level flight just means lift = weight and thrust = drag — a constant, moving balance.
A wing only makes lift while air flows past it fast enough — stop moving, and lift vanishes.
This is why fixed-wing planes can't hover — a helicopter's spinning rotor blades solve that problem differently.
chunks.key_takeaway: Flight is a constant, moving balance between four forces — lift vs weight, and thrust vs drag.

key_terms.definition: The backward force of air resistance pushing against a moving plane, always fighting against thrust.
The forward force an engine or propeller produces to push a plane through the air.

chunks.heading: Steering with no steering wheel
chunks.idea: A plane has no wheels gripping a road, so a pilot can't just point the front sideways. Instead, small hinged flaps on the wings and tail change how much lift different parts of the plane make, tipping the whole aircraft where it needs to go.
chunks.detail:
With no road to grip, a plane can't steer by pointing a front wheel. Instead, pilots steer by deliberately tipping the whole aircraft, using small flaps built into the wings and tail.

Ailerons sit at the back edge of each wing and tilt in opposite directions — one edges up while the other edges down — making one wing produce more lift than the other. That rolls the plane sideways, like tipping a tray.

The elevator, a flap on the horizontal tail, tilts the plane's nose up or down. That motion is called pitch, and it's how a plane climbs, descends, or points where it's about to go.

The rudder, a flap on the vertical tail fin, swings the nose left or right — called yaw. It's mostly used together with a roll, to smooth out a turn, rather than by itself.

So a plane actually turns more like a bicycle than a car — mostly by leaning, or rolling, into the turn, with the rudder just nudging the nose to keep everything coordinated, rather than by swiveling like a car's front wheels.
chunks.example: Watch an airliner bank into a turn from the ground and you'll see one wingtip dip lower than the other before the nose visibly swings. That dip is the ailerons rolling the plane, and it happens first — exactly like a cyclist leaning into a curve before the bike's path actually bends.
points: Ailerons, on the wings, roll the plane side to side by making one wing lift more than the other.
The elevator, on the tail, pitches the nose up or down.
The rudder, on the tail fin, yaws the nose left or right, mostly to smooth out a turn.
A plane turns more like a leaning bicycle than a steering car — it banks first, then curves.
chunks.key_takeaway: Pilots don't turn a wheel — they tilt small flaps that change lift on different parts of the plane, tipping the whole aircraft where they want it to go.

key_terms.definition: Hinged flaps on the trailing edge of each wing that move opposite each other to roll the plane.
The three ways a plane can rotate: tipping side to side (roll), nose up or down (pitch), and nose left or right (yaw).

chunks.heading: Now you'll see wings everywhere
chunks.idea: Once you understand "tilt a surface, throw a moving fluid one way, get shoved back the other way," you'll start noticing it isn't just an airplane trick. It's hiding in birds, frisbees, and even race cars.
chunks.detail:
A bird's wing works on exactly the same principle as a jet's wing. It's tilted and curved, throwing air down and behind with every wingbeat — which is also why birds bank into turns by tilting one wing, just like an airliner does.

A thrown frisbee is a small spinning wing. Tilt it slightly as you throw it, and it throws air downward the same way an airplane wing does, which is part of why it glides gracefully instead of dropping like an ordinary disc.

Flip the whole idea upside down and you get downforce instead of lift. A race car's rear spoiler is shaped and tilted like an upside-down wing, throwing air upward instead of down — so by Newton's same rule, the air shoves the car downward onto the track instead of lifting it off, giving the tires extra grip.

Even a sailboat's sail, angled into the wind, is using a version of this same trick to turn moving air into a useful push. Once you know the pattern — a tilted surface meeting a moving fluid — you start spotting it in dozens of everyday objects.

So the next time you watch a bird bank in the sky, or a frisbee curve across a park, or a race car grip a tight corner, you'll know exactly what's happening underneath: the same quiet trick that lifts a 400-ton jet, working at a completely different scale.
chunks.example: Next time you see a Formula 1 car, look at the wing-shaped piece sticking up at the back. It's deliberately built and tilted like an upside-down airplane wing, throwing air upward so that the reaction shoves the car downward onto the road — letting it corner far faster without flying off the track.
points: A bird's wing generates lift the same way a plane's does — tilt, curve, throw air down.
A frisbee is a small spinning wing, tilted slightly to throw air down as it flies.
Flip the trick upside down and you get downforce: a race car's spoiler pushes air up so the reaction pushes the car down.
Once you know the pattern — tilted surface meets moving fluid — you'll start noticing it everywhere.
chunks.key_takeaway: The same trick that lifts a 400-ton jet also glides a frisbee, banks a bird, and grips a race car to the road — a tilted surface, meeting moving fluid, redirecting it to push back.

key_terms.definition: A downward push created the same way as lift but flipped upside down — used by race cars to press their tires harder onto the track.

recap: Wings don't fly by brute engine power — they tilt into oncoming air and throw it downward, and by Newton's third law the air throws the wing back up as lift.
The popular "air must meet up at the same time" explanation of lift is a myth NASA itself calls out — the real story is a wing deflecting air and Newton's third law pushing back.
Tilt (angle of attack) is the main lift dial, but push it too far and airflow breaks away from the wing — that sudden loss of lift is called a stall.
Flight is a constant balance of four forces (lift vs weight, thrust vs drag), and pilots steer not with a wheel but by tilting small flaps that roll, pitch, and yaw the whole plane.

check.question: Your friend says a plane's wings work because air has to travel over the curved top and flat bottom of the wing and "meet up" at the back at the same time, so the air on top has to move faster, and that speed is what creates lift. What's actually wrong with this explanation, and what really makes a wing produce lift?
check.answer: This is the popular but inaccurate "equal transit time" explanation — the air streams above and below a wing don't actually need to reunite at the tail at all, and NASA's own aerodynamics engineers say this story is not correct. What really produces lift is that the wing is tilted, at its angle of attack, so it deflects the passing air downward; by Newton's third law, that air pushes back on the wing with an equal and opposite force — upward. That push-back is lift.

parts.next_up: One machine left, and it's the one you touch without ever seeing it: Part 5 follows electricity from the moment it's generated to the instant it reaches the switch on your wall.

parts.recap_so_far: You've now taken apart four machines: the engine that turns burning fuel into motion, the fridge that moves heat instead of making cold, the phone that turns a tap into an answer in a blink, and the wing that throws air down to hold hundreds of tons in the sky. Today you're closing the course with the biggest machine of them all — one so large you've never once seen the whole thing, even though you touch it every single day.

chunks.heading: The largest machine ever built
chunks.idea: The power grid is often called the biggest machine humans have ever built — millions of miles of wire linking power plants to your wall socket. And it has one strange rule that makes it unlike almost anything else you own: it cannot save electricity for later.
chunks.detail: Think about your phone. It stores power in a battery, so you can charge it at night and use it all day. The grid, for the most part, doesn't get that luxury — barely any of the electricity flowing through it is sitting in storage anywhere.
chunks.example: Picture a city's grid on a scorching afternoon when everyone switches on air conditioning at once. Somewhere, right that second, a power plant has to burn more fuel or spin a turbine faster to cover that exact new demand — there's no giant warehouse of spare electricity to dip into.
points: The grid links power plants to homes through millions of miles of wire — one continuous, connected machine.
Almost no electricity in it is stored — it has to be made in the same instant it's used.
This "make it now" rule is the hidden constraint behind everything else about how the grid is built and run.
chunks.key_takeaway: Unlike almost everything else you own, the grid can't save power for later — it has to be made the instant you need it.

key_terms.definition: The connected network of power plants, wires, and equipment that generates electricity and delivers it to homes and businesses.

chunks.heading: One trick, a hundred disguises
chunks.idea: Coal, gas, nuclear, wind, hydro, solar — these sound like completely different ways to make electricity. But strip away the fuel, and almost all of them (solar panels being the big exception) are doing the exact same physical trick: spinning a magnet next to a coil of wire.
chunks.detail: Back in the 1830s, a scientist named Michael Faraday found something strange: if you move a magnet near a loop of wire, electrons in that wire start to flow, with no battery involved at all. That effect is called electromagnetic induction, and it's still the workhorse behind most of the world's electricity nearly two centuries later.
chunks.example: A coal plant burns coal to boil water into high-pressure steam, and that steam shoves a turbine — a big fan-like wheel — around and around. That spinning turbine turns a magnet inside a generator, and the spinning magnet is what actually creates the electric current, exactly like Faraday's experiment, just done at a massive industrial scale.
points: Electromagnetic induction: moving a magnet near a coil of wire pushes electrons through the wire, making electricity.
Coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, and wind plants mostly differ only in what spins the turbine — steam, falling water, or moving air.
Solar panels are the odd one out — they make electricity straight from sunlight, no spinning involved.
One 1830s discovery still quietly powers almost everything you plug in today.
chunks.key_takeaway: Most power plants don't create electricity from scratch — they just find a different way to spin a magnet next to a coil of wire.

key_terms.definition: The effect, discovered by Michael Faraday, where moving a magnet near a wire coil pushes an electric current through it.
A wheel with blades that spins when pushed by steam, water, or air, turning that motion into the spin a generator needs.

chunks.heading: Why power lines carry deadly voltage
chunks.idea: Electricity leaves a power plant at a voltage far higher than anything in your house — high enough to be lethal near the wire. That's not a design flaw. It's a deliberate trick to keep the electricity from wasting itself away as heat before it ever reaches you.
chunks.detail:
Wires aren't perfect. As current — the actual flow of electrons — pushes through a wire, some of that energy always leaks out as heat, the same way a phone charger cable gets slightly warm.

The amount of energy wasted this way grows with the square of the current, meaning even a small drop in current cuts the waste a lot. So engineers use a device called a transformer to push the voltage way up right as power leaves the plant, which — for the same amount of total power — lets the current traveling down the line drop dramatically.

That's why you'll see power lines strung between huge steel towers, held far from the ground and from each other: the voltage running through them is genuinely dangerous, exactly because it was cranked up on purpose.

Once that high-voltage electricity finally nears your neighborhood, a second transformer does the opposite job, stepping the voltage back down in stages until it's safe and steady enough to run a toaster.
chunks.example: Sending power at a very high voltage lets the current stay low enough for wires no thicker than your finger to carry it hundreds of miles without melting or wasting most of the energy as heat along the way. Try shoving that same power down the line at your home's low household voltage instead, and the current would be so high the wires would waste enormous amounts of energy as heat, and could overheat.
points: Wires always waste a little energy as heat, and that waste grows fast as current goes up.
Stepping voltage way up right after generation lets current — and the wasted heat — stay low over long distances.
This is exactly why big transmission lines look and feel dangerous: the high voltage is deliberate, not accidental.
Transformers near your home step the voltage back down in stages before it ever reaches an outlet.
chunks.key_takeaway: Power travels cross-country at extremely high voltage on purpose — it's the trick that keeps long-distance electricity from wasting itself away as heat.

key_terms.definition: A device with no moving parts that raises or lowers electrical voltage, used to send power efficiently and then make it safe for home use.
The actual flow of electrons through a wire — the thing that generates wasted heat, which is why engineers work hard to keep it low on long lines.

chunks.heading: A tightrope walk, every second of every day
chunks.idea: Because the grid can't store electricity, grid operators have to keep the total power being made exactly equal to the total power being used, every single second, all day and all night. Get it wrong for too long, and the lights can go out across an entire region.
chunks.detail:
Every grid runs at a steady electrical rhythm, either 50 or 60 cycles per second depending on the country, called its frequency. That rhythm barely moves when supply and demand are matched — but the instant they drift apart, even slightly, the frequency itself starts to drift too.

Too much power being made compared to what's being used, and the frequency creeps up. Too little power, and it sags down. So grid operators treat frequency almost like a patient's pulse — a live, second-by-second readout of whether the whole system is in balance.

If that drift ever gets too large, power plants and safety equipment start automatically disconnecting themselves to protect their own machinery from damage. That's a good thing for each individual plant, but it removes even more supply from an already-struggling grid.

That's how a small, local problem can spiral: one imbalance trips a few plants offline, which throws the balance further off, which trips more plants offline — a cascading failure that can black out a whole region within minutes, even though it started from something fairly small.
chunks.example: This is exactly why a heat wave is dangerous for a grid, not just for people. Air conditioners across an entire city switch on together, demand spikes faster than plants can ramp up to match it, and if operators can't bring extra supply online quickly enough, frequency drifts and rolling blackouts get ordered on purpose — to protect the wider grid from an uncontrolled, larger collapse.
points: Grid frequency (50 or 60 cycles per second) is a live signal of whether supply and demand are balanced.
Too much power pushes frequency up; too little pulls it down.
A big enough imbalance makes power plants disconnect automatically to protect themselves — which can make the imbalance worse.
That chain reaction is how a small local glitch can cascade into a large-scale blackout.
chunks.key_takeaway: Because electricity can't be stored, grid operators have to match supply to demand every second — and frequency is the number that tells them if they're failing.

key_terms.definition: The steady electrical rhythm (50 or 60 cycles per second) of a power grid, which rises or falls depending on whether supply and demand are in balance.
A chain reaction where one part of the grid failing pushes more of the system out of balance, tripping further failures until a blackout spreads.

chunks.heading: The last mile, ending at your wall
chunks.idea: By the time electricity has crossed the transmission grid at high voltage, it still has to make one more journey: down through your neighborhood, into your house, and out through the socket that just felt completely ordinary a second ago.
chunks.detail:
Once high-voltage electricity nears a town, it enters a substation, where transformers knock the voltage down to a medium level suitable for local distribution lines — the shorter, thinner wires you actually see running along streets on wooden poles.

A final small transformer, often that gray cylindrical can mounted on a nearby pole or a green box on the ground, steps the voltage down one last time to the level your home's wiring is built to handle safely.

From there, wiring inside your walls carries it to every outlet, and a meter — old-style spinning disk or a modern digital one — quietly counts how much you've used, which is what your electricity bill is actually built from.

When you plug something in and switch it on, you complete a circuit that traces back, transformer by transformer, all the way to a spinning turbine that might be dozens or hundreds of miles away — turning at that very instant partly because you just asked it to.
chunks.example: Look up next time you're walking down a residential street and you'll likely spot a gray cylindrical can partway up a wooden pole — that's a distribution transformer, doing the final voltage step-down for a handful of nearby houses before the wires dive down to their meters.
points: Substations step voltage down from transmission level to a medium distribution level near towns.
A final small transformer, often on a utility pole, steps voltage down again to household level.
A meter at your home measures how much electricity you actually use — the basis of your bill.
Flipping a switch completes a circuit stretching back to a spinning generator, possibly hundreds of miles away.
chunks.key_takeaway: The electricity in your wall socket has already passed through several transformers, each one bringing it a step closer to safe and usable — the very last leg of a journey that may have started hundreds of miles away.

key_terms.definition: A facility where transformers and switching equipment step voltage down (or up) as electricity moves between the transmission grid and local distribution lines.
The shorter, lower-voltage power lines that carry electricity the final stretch from a substation to individual homes and businesses.

chunks.heading: The switch you'll never look at the same way
chunks.idea: You now know that flipping a light switch quietly asks a turbine somewhere to spin a little faster, and asks an entire continent-spanning machine to hold its balance for you. That single fact explains a surprising number of headlines you'll now actually understand.
chunks.detail:
Wind and solar power are wonderful for one big reason: they burn no fuel. But they're genuinely tricky for a grid built on the "make it now, match it exactly" rule you just learned, because the sun sets and the wind dies down on its own schedule, not the grid's.

That's why you'll increasingly hear about grid-scale batteries — warehouses of the same lithium-ion technology in your phone, but sized to smooth out a few hours of mismatch between when solar and wind are generating and when people actually need power.

It's also why electric vehicles are more than just a car story. Millions of EVs charging at once are a genuinely new, large source of demand that grid operators now have to plan the balancing act around.

And it's exactly why you occasionally read about a whole country or region going dark: somewhere in that giant, invisible machine, the delicate second-by-second balance of supply and demand tipped further than the system could absorb.

That's the real thread running through this entire course, not just today's session: an engine, a fridge, a phone, a wing, a grid — each one felt like effortless, silent magic, until you looked underneath and found nothing but a small number of clever, physical tricks, applied at a scale big enough to run the modern world.
chunks.example: The next time you read that a country suffered a widespread blackout, look for the word "frequency" in the reporting — it's often right there, the exact signal from today's lesson, the grid's pulse having drifted too far before operators could restore the balance.
points: Wind and solar are clean but variable, which strains a grid built to balance supply and demand instant by instant.
Grid-scale batteries and EV charging are both reshaping that balancing act in real time.
Large blackouts almost always trace back to the same root cause: a supply-demand imbalance the system couldn't recover from in time.
Every machine in this course — engine, fridge, phone, wing, grid — turned out to be a handful of clever physical tricks, not magic.
chunks.key_takeaway: The grid's simple, unbreakable rule — make exactly what's being used, every second — is the hidden reason behind renewable energy's biggest challenge and most blackout headlines you'll ever read.

key_terms.definition: A large battery installation connected to the grid, used to store extra power for a few hours to smooth out gaps between generation and demand.

recap: The grid can't store electricity at scale, so power has to be generated in the same instant it's used.
Most power plants — coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, wind — make electricity the same way: spinning a magnet next to a coil of wire, a trick called electromagnetic induction.
Voltage is deliberately pushed sky-high for the journey across the grid to cut wasted heat, then stepped back down through transformers before it reaches your home.
Grid frequency is the live signal of whether supply matches demand — and a bad enough imbalance can cascade into a region-wide blackout.

check.question: Why can't a power grid just make a bit more electricity than it needs and store the extra for later, the way your phone stores extra battery?
check.answer: Because the grid has almost no bulk storage — unlike a phone battery, the electricity flowing through the wires has to be generated in the same instant it's consumed. That's why grid operators constantly watch frequency, the grid's live "pulse," and adjust generation second by second to keep supply and demand matched, rather than just overproducing and stockpiling the extra.
